title: We Want to Love Human Storytelling, But AI Is Simply More Engaging, Study Shows
excerpt: New research finds that people prefer stories written by AI—especially when they believe humans wrote them.
content_html:
Not only are people unable to tell the difference between stories written by humans or artificial intelligence, they actually prefer it when the stories are created by AI. And that’s especially true when they are told that the stories had human authors, according to a new study from Villanova University.

The study consisted of multiple experiments, all of which indicated a preference for AI. In the first, 1,682 participants were told to rate both the quality of six short stories they were given and how “engaging” they were. They were told, either correctly or incorrectly, who or what had authored each one. 

Not only were AI-generated stories found to be higher-quality (by 6%) and more engaging (by 8%), they were rated “even more highly,” researchers concluded, when participants believed that they were written by humans (by an additional 3%).

Deena Weisberg, the senior author of the study and an associate professor from Villanova’s Department of Psychological & Brain Sciences, said in a press release that the finding “reveals a bias towards narratives written by real people.”

That may be because “we assume creative writing requires uniquely human qualities, such as emotional understanding and lived experience,” she said, explaining that it shows how “public assumptions about AI's capabilities are increasingly out of date.”

Furthermore, people were only able to identify AI-generated content roughly 40% and 52% of the time in two subsequent experiments, each with over 400 participants. People who said they were AI-literate had more success than people who claimed to have a background in literature. 

“Familiarity with AI systems appeared to help people recognize the patterns typical of AI-generated writing, such as em dashes and sentence structures such as ‘it’s not just X, it’s Y,’” Weisberg said. “That suggests that improving AI literacy would be one way to help people to navigate the new AI-enabled world that we’re living in.”

Cameron Jones, assistant professor of psychology at Stony Brook University tells TIME that the study’s findings are not necessarily surprising, considering the history of research going back years that shows people’s diminishing ability to tell between artificial intelligence and humans. 

He also points to the trajectory of his own studies, which look at whether people can differentiate between them in conversation. In those scenarios, he says, “The person actually gets to quiz the model and ask follow-up questions.” 

Even then, they had trouble distinguishing between human and generative content partners.

Jones says that this is because the large language models driving the content responses are trained to appeal to users.

“We basically get the model to generate little bits of text, and then we get people to read them, and they give a thumbs up if they like what the model's saying and they give a thumbs down if they don't like what the model's saying,” he says. 

It’s no surprise that people prefer the results, he explains, when “we're optimizing these models' outputs against our preferences.”

It can oversimplify output, but it leads to writing with higher overall appeal—whereas humans might write something truly exceptional that only caters to select tastes.

“Real humans are weird and idiosyncratic, and they're very different from one another,” Jones says. “But models can kind of learn to be this kind of milquetoast everyman who appeals to everybody.”

While the findings align with rising exposure to artificial intelligence, along with algorithmic reward systems for broadly approachable content on platforms like TikTok, Weisberg does not think that the current digital landscape is to blame for the results. She says, “Technologies amplify existing tendencies, rather than creating them.”

Plus, she adds, the human-authored content might have simply challenged readers more.

“AI writing tends to be clearer, more direct and easier to process,” she said. And it’s reasonable for participants to find themselves more deeply engaged with content that offers greater predictability and less friction. 

In other words, Weisberg says, “Difficult or subtle material requires more brainpower.”

content_html_zh:
人们不仅无法区分人类编写的故事和人工智能编写的故事，而且实际上他们更喜欢人工智能创建的故事。 根据维拉诺瓦大学的一项新研究，当他们被告知这些故事有人类作者时，情况尤其如此。

该研究由多项实验组成，所有这些实验都表明了人们对人工智能的偏好。 在第一个实验中，1,682 名参与者被要求对他们收到的六个短篇故事的质量以及它们的“吸引力”进行评分。 他们被告知，无论是正确还是错误，每一篇文章的作者是谁或是什么。

研究人员得出结论，人工智能生成的故事不仅质量更高（提高了 6%）、更具吸引力（提高了 8%），而且当参与者相信这些故事是由人类编写的时（额外提高了 3%），它们的评分“甚至更高”。

该研究的资深作者、维拉诺瓦大学心理与脑科学系副教授迪娜·韦斯伯格(Deena Weisberg)在一份新闻稿中表示，这一发现“揭示了人们对真实人物撰写的叙述存在偏见”。

她说，这可能是因为“我们认为创意写作需要独特的人类品质，例如情感理解和生活经验”，并解释说这表明“公众对人工智能能力的假设越来越过时”。

此外，在随后的两次实验中，每个实验都有超过 400 名参与者，人们只能在大约 40% 和 52% 的时间内识别人工智能生成的内容。 自称懂人工智能的人比自称有文学背景的人更成功。

“熟悉人工智能系统似乎可以帮助人们识别人工智能生成的写作的典型模式，例如破折号和句子结构，例如‘这不仅仅是 X，这是 Y’，”Weisberg 说。 “这表明，提高人工智能素养将是帮助人们驾驭我们所生活的人工智能新世界的一种方式。”

石溪大学心理学助理教授卡梅伦·琼斯 (Cameron Jones) 告诉《时代》杂志，考虑到多年前的研究历史表明人们区分人工智能和人类的能力正在减弱，这项研究的结果并不一定令人惊讶。

他还指出了自己的研究轨迹，即人们是否能够在谈话中区分它们。 他说，在这种情况下，“人们实际上可以测试模型并提出后续问题。”

即便如此，他们也很难区分人类和生成内容合作伙伴。

琼斯说，这是因为驱动内容响应的大型语言模型经过训练以吸引用户。

“我们基本上让模型生成一些文本，然后让人们阅读它们，如果他们喜欢模型所说的内容，他们就会竖起大拇指，如果他们不喜欢模型所说的内容，他们就会竖起大拇指，”他说。

他解释说，当“我们根据我们的偏好优化这些模型的输出”时，人们更喜欢结果也就不足为奇了。

它可能会过度简化输出，但它会导致写作具有更高的整体吸引力——而人类可能会写出一些真正出色的东西，只迎合特定的口味。

“真正的人类是怪异和独特的，他们彼此之间非常不同，”琼斯说。 “但是模特们可以学会成为那种对每个人都有吸引力的、胆怯的普通人。”

虽然这些发现与人工智能的曝光度不断增加以及 TikTok 等平台上广泛普及的内容的算法奖励系统相一致，但韦斯伯格并不认为当前的数字环境是造成这一结果的原因。 她说：“技术放大了现有趋势，而不是创造它们。”

另外，她补充道，人类创作的内容可能只是对读者提出了更多挑战。

“人工智能写作往往更清晰、更直接、更容易处理，”她说。 参与者发现自己更深入地参与提供更高可预测性和更少摩擦的内容是合理的。

换句话说，韦斯伯格说，“困难或微妙的材料需要更多的脑力。”
